items.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025
items.q: I’ve heard music teachers put down Louis Armstrong for example... learn all these bebop scales and imitate Charlie Parker and John Coltrane and that’s real jazz you know.

ctx.x: Yeah. It’s good. And he mentions some things about the novelty, the way people played novelty songs and all that, and he doesn’t apologize for anything. It was like this is what it was and everybody was looking for their own voice and trying to please an audience. And I’m wondering if you think that current jazz education gives early jazz its due?

Generally no. When I came up I started playing in the 1970s, one of the surprising things that I discovered was how much music education fluffs off early jazz. And this goes not only down to the literature but actual music teachers and programs. And they all have it put under the label of Dixieland, which implies something corny, invalid, not musical, and of course a lot of the music teachers were modern jazz players or failed modern jazz players, and they, you know they promoted what they liked. And, you know I…

embryonic form of noise that wasn’t really valid. I’ve heard music teachers put down Louis Armstrong for example, saying he couldn’t really play and this kind of stuff, and make jokes about him, make jokes about early jazz and early jazz musicians. So I had to kind of suffer through that prejudice against early jazz music and come to my own understanding of what the music was and what it meant. And fortunately I discovered and was able to interact with these older musicians who, you know, I was one of them…
